clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the liver isoform (CPT1A) of carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 on the outer mitochondrial membrane, the enzyme that initiates entry of long-chain fatty acids into mitochondria by esterifying them to carnitine.
Presents with fasting-induced hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, raised transaminases and a Reye-like encephalopathy, typically triggered by an intercurrent illness.

Unlike carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 or translocase defects, the heart and skeletal muscle are characteristically spared, so cardiomyopathy and rhabdomyolysis are absent because muscle relies on a different isoform.

The biochemistry is paradoxical among fatty-acid-oxidation disorders: free carnitine is normal or elevated with low long-chain acylcarnitines, giving a raised ratio of free carnitine to combined palmitoyl- and stearoylcarnitine.
Renal tubular acidosis may accompany metabolic crises.
A common CPT1A variant (p.Pro479Leu) is highly prevalent in Arctic Indigenous populations and is linked to infant hypoglycaemia and sudden unexpected death.

Treatment centres on strict fasting avoidance, a high-carbohydrate diet with long-chain-fat restriction and medium-chain triglyceride supplementation, plus a glucose-based emergency regimen during illness.
reference.pathophysiology: Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1A sits on the outer mitochondrial membrane and catalyses the rate-controlling, malonyl-CoA-sensitive step of long-chain fatty-acid import, converting long-chain acyl-CoA plus carnitine into acylcarnitine that the translocase can carry inwards. When CPT1A activity is lost, hepatic long-chain fatty-acid oxidation cannot proceed, so during fasting the liver fails to generate ketones and to sustain gluconeogenesis, producing hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and a Reye-like encephalopathy. Because the enzymatic block is upstream of acylcarnitine formation, long-chain acylcarnitines are conspicuously low while free carnitine accumulates, the mirror image of most fatty-acid-oxidation defects. The muscle and cardiac isoform CPT1B is unaffected, which is why the heart and skeletal muscle are clinically spared, and impaired transporter function in the renal tubule can produce a tubular acidosis.
additionalDifferentials: Medium-chain and very long-chain acyl-CoA dehydrogenase deficiency
Carnitine palmitoyltransferase 2 and carnitine-acylcarnitine translocase deficiency (with cardiac and muscle features)
Congenital hyperinsulinism and other endocrine causes of hypoglycaemia
Gluconeogenesis defects such as fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase deficiency
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing low long-chain species with high free carnitine and a raised free-carnitine to long-chain-acylcarnitine ratio
Urine organic acids during crisis demonstrating inappropriately low ketones
Paired blood glucose and ketone monitoring during intercurrent illness
Enzyme activity assay in cultured fibroblasts
Assessment of renal tubular function and acid-base status
redFlags: Acute liver dysfunction and hepatomegaly during illness
Sudden unexplained infant deterioration, especially in high-prevalence Arctic populations
reference.prognosis: With early diagnosis, avoidance of fasting and dietary management the prognosis is generally good and cardiac or muscle complications do not develop; the main hazard is an unrecognised hypoglycaemic crisis.
pitfalls: Misreading the low-acylcarnitine, high-free-carnitine profile as normal or as carnitine excess
Expecting cardiomyopathy or rhabdomyolysis, whose absence does not argue against this long-chain defect
Overlooking an accompanying renal tubular acidosis
Under-recognising the founder variant and its sudden-death risk in Arctic Indigenous populations
references: Fatty acid oxidation disorder management consensus guidelines
management: Prevent hypoglycaemic crises by avoiding fasting and ensuring frequent carbohydrate intake, with a written emergency regimen during intercurrent illness
Restrict long-chain fat and supplement with medium-chain triglycerides, which enter mitochondria independently of the carnitine cycle
Treat acute decompensation with intravenous glucose to restore euglycaemia and reverse the Reye-like state
Recognise and correct any associated renal tubular acidosis during crises
Monitor with paired glucose and ketone measurement during illness and periodic acylcarnitine profiling
Manage within a specialist metabolic team
Offer CPT1A genetic testing, counselling and family or newborn screening, noting the high-prevalence Arctic variant
